name: Submit and update outage schedules with the AESO
summary: Alberta's system operator needs to know when every generating asset of 5 MW or more will be out of service so it can check there is enough supply. The outage planners collect planned outages and changes from the gas, hydro and wind sites, check them for conflicts and market timing, get them approved and enter them in the AESO Energy Trading System, refreshing the full 24-month list every month and explaining any change made less than 3 months ahead. They also answer AESO requests to move outages when supply is tight. The work is slow because site details, market reviews and approvals queue behind other work, and error-prone because the same outage is kept in several places.

baseline.org_archetype: An Alberta merchant generator with about 30 separately offered gas, hydro, wind and battery assets that the AESO requires to report outages.
baseline.notes: ISO rule 306.5 was in force throughout 2019-2022 with the same requirements; the 2020-09-16 revision added timing for delayed forced outages.

trigger: A site or the major outage team sends a new or changed planned outage, the month-end 24-month refresh falls due, a repair needs a delayed forced outage, or the AESO asks for outages to be reviewed.
end_state: The outage is in the Energy Trading System, checked against the AESO reports and in the internal schedule sent to the desk; or the outage is kept after an AESO request; or a cancellation claim is filed.

volume.seasonality: Peaks before the spring and autumn outage seasons, when major outage plans are fixed, and at each month-end refresh.

evidence.note: The rule requires a monthly 24-month submission plus every revision; about 30 reporting assets with about 4 planned outages starting a month, each revised several times, gives about 30 submissions a month (estimate).
Submission duties follow the rule; share of the 12 planners estimated.
Approvals and AESO requests; share estimated.

steps.name: Log the outage change
steps.description: The outage planner receives an outage plan or change from a site, the major outage team or the AESO, logs it in the outage tracking spreadsheet with the asset, dates and MW, and decides which kind of submission it is.

next.condition: delayed forced outage starting within days
AESO asks to review an outage

evidence.note: The rule's four submission types (planned, monthly 24-month list, delayed forced, ISO request); mix estimated.

steps.name: Ask the site for the outage details
steps.description: The planner emails or phones the site's maintenance planner for the exact start and end times, the MW that will be unavailable (whole unit or derate) and a plain description of the work, which the rule requires in the submission.

evidence.note: Dates, times, durations, MW impact and nature of work from s.3(1).

steps.name: Confirm dates, MW and scope at the site
steps.description: The site maintenance planner checks the work orders, crew bookings and contractor dates behind the outage and replies with the confirmed window, the MW impact and the work to be done.

error.defect_description: Window or MW does not match the crew and contractor bookings.

evidence.note: Site reply time estimated. The thermal maintenance planner stands for hydro and wind site planners, who also report outages of 5 MW or more.

steps.name: Check conflicts with other outages
steps.description: The planner places the outage in the outage scheduling software against other units' outages, specialist crew and crane bookings, transmission outages posted by the AESO and the same site's other units, and flags overlaps.

error.defect_description: An overlap with a crew booking or another unit is missed.

evidence.note: Common planning practice; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Review market timing
steps.description: The portfolio optimisation analyst checks the forward price curve and the hedge position for the outage window and asks for a move when the outage falls in a high-price period that a nearby low-price window could avoid.

evidence.note: An optimisation team formed in 2021 to schedule production toward high-price periods; move share estimated.

steps.name: Draft the ETS outage entry
steps.description: The planner prepares the entry: asset, Derate-Planned or Outage-Planned, start and end times, available MW during the outage and a short nature-of-work note, and checks whether the outage now starts within 3 months.

next.condition: submitted later than 3 months before the start

evidence.note: Designations and fields from s.3(1); late-change share estimated.

steps.name: Write the late-change reason
steps.description: Because the change is submitted less than 3 months before the outage starts, the planner writes a statement of why the outage differs from the original submission or was not in the monthly list, such as a new defect or a contractor change.

control.basis: AESO ISO rule 306.5 s.3(4) (reasons for changes later than 3 months before the outage)

evidence.note: Reason statement required by s.3(4).

steps.name: Approve the submission
steps.description: The outage manager reviews the draft entry, the conflict check and the market timing view, and approves it or sends it back with questions.

control.basis: Internal review of regulatory submissions before filing

evidence.note: Internal approval practice; wait estimated.

steps.name: Enter the outage in the Energy Trading System
steps.description: The planner logs into the AESO Energy Trading System under the pool participant's account and enters or edits the outage record with its designation, times, MW and nature of work.

error.defect_description: Wrong MW, time zone or end time keyed.

control.basis: AESO ISO rule 306.5 s.2(3) and s.3 (planned outage information through the ETS)

evidence.note: Submission through the Energy Trading System from s.2(3) and the information document.

steps.name: AESO posts the outage in its reports
steps.description: The Energy Trading System stores the record and the AESO's daily, monthly and 7-day available capability reports pick it up at their next update, usually within 5 to 10 minutes.

evidence.note: Report update interval of 5 to 10 minutes, at most 20, from the information document.

steps.name: Check the record and the AESO report
steps.description: The planner reopens the record on the ETS outage scheduling tab, compares it with the approved entry and checks the change shows in the AESO monthly or 7-day report.

evidence.note: Checking the Outage Scheduling tab is the information document's suggested check; error share estimated.

steps.name: Update the internal outage schedule
steps.description: The planner updates the outage in the company outage scheduling software and the tracking spreadsheet, retyping the dates and MW so the internal schedule matches what the AESO now holds.

error.defect_description: Internal schedule left out of step with the ETS.

evidence.note: Re-keying between ETS and internal tools was common; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Tell the desk and forecasting
steps.description: The planner emails the updated schedule to the real-time desk, the forecasting analysts and the site so offers, generation forecasts and hedges reflect the outage.

evidence.note: Distribution practice; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Sample the record for compliance
steps.description: The market compliance officer takes a sample of outage submissions, checks they were filed on time, with reasons where late, and match the plant logs, and files the evidence for a possible Market Surveillance Administrator review.

control.basis: Company market compliance program over ISO rules enforced by the Market Surveillance Administrator

evidence.note: Sampling rate and timing estimated; the MSA enforces ISO rule compliance.

steps.name: Compile the 24-month outage list
steps.description: Before the first day of the month the planner collects planned outages for the next 24 months from every gas, hydro, wind and battery asset of 5 MW or more, from the major outage plans and site maintenance plans.

control.basis: AESO ISO rule 306.5 s.3(2) (planned outages for the next 24 months by the 1st of each month)

evidence.note: Monthly 24-month submission by the first day of each month from s.3(2); effort estimated.

steps.name: Reconcile the list with the ETS
steps.description: The planner compares the 24-month list line by line with the outage records already in the ETS and marks records to add, change or cancel.

error.defect_description: A cancelled outage is left in the ETS.

evidence.note: Reconciliation practice; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Read the AESO request
steps.description: The outage manager reads the AESO notice or call: the AESO has posted a supply adequacy or reliability concern for a period and asks participants to review outages planned in it.

evidence.note: Posting for at least one week and direct contact with participants under s.7(5) and 7(6).

steps.name: Assess whether the outage can move
steps.description: The outage manager and planner check what moving the outage would do to contractors, specialist crews, parts deliveries, manufacturer service agreements, the hedge position and equipment risk, and choose dates that could work.

evidence.note: Assessment effort estimated.

steps.name: Reply to the AESO
steps.description: The outage manager phones or emails the AESO with what the company can do: move the outage, shorten it or keep it, and why.

evidence.note: Cancellation directive possible only after the s.7 steps and CEO authorisation; shares estimated and directives were rare.

steps.name: Prepare the cancellation submissions and cost claim
steps.description: After a cancellation directive the planner writes a detailed description of the cancelled work with the equipment involved and an estimate of incremental costs, then assembles the claim with invoices and calculations within 40 days of the settlement period.

control.basis: AESO ISO rule 306.5 s.8 and s.11 (cancellation submissions and incremental cost claims)

evidence.note: Work description and cost estimate under s.8(1) and claim within 40 days under s.11(2).

steps.name: Phone the AESO about a delayed forced outage
steps.description: When equipment must come out of service within the next day for a repair that cannot wait for a planned outage, the real-time trader calls the AESO's recorded line, then the planner follows with the ETS entry designated Derate-Forced or Outage-Forced.

control.basis: AESO ISO rule 306.5 s.4 (delayed forced outage notification)

evidence.note: Telephone notice on a recorded line when less than 24 hours' notice under s.4(2); ETS designation under s.4(1).

exceptions.name: Late change
exceptions.description: A change submitted less than 3 months before the outage needs a written reason in the submission.

exceptions.name: Market timing move
exceptions.description: The optimisation analyst asks to move an outage out of a high-price window and the planner re-checks conflicts.

exceptions.name: AESO asks to review an outage
exceptions.description: The AESO posts a supply adequacy concern and asks participants to review outages; the company moves, shortens or keeps its outage.

exceptions.name: Cancellation directive
exceptions.description: The AESO cancels the outage by directive; the company files the work description and an incremental cost claim.

exceptions.name: Keying error
exceptions.description: The ETS record does not match the approved entry and is corrected.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from request received to submission verified
benchmarks.population: Planned outage submissions and changes at an Alberta generator

evidence.note: Estimate: site replies and approvals take one to three working days each; the monthly refresh waits for month-end.

benchmarks.unit: months ahead covered by the monthly submission
benchmarks.population: Alberta generating source assets of 5 MW or more

benchmarks.unit: months before outage start after which a reason is required

pain_points.description: The same outage is held in the site schedule, the outage scheduling software, a tracking spreadsheet and the ETS, and is re-keyed between them.

evidence.note: Common practice in 2019-2022; estimate.

pain_points.description: Site replies and approvals queue behind other work, so changes often land inside the 3-month window and need a written reason.

evidence.note: The 3-month reason rule is in s.3(4); queue times estimated.

pain_points.description: Moving an outage at the AESO's request ripples through contractor, crew and manufacturer bookings that were fixed months earlier.

evidence.note: Estimate.

sources.title: ISO Rules Part 300, Section 306.5 Generation Outage Reporting and Coordination (effective 2023-01-01)
sources.supports: Applies to pool participants with generating source assets of 5 MW or more (wind included since 2015); outage changes of 5 MW or more must be reported; submissions through the Energy Trading System; planned outages designated Derate-Planned or Outage-Planned with dates, times, MW impact and nature of work; by the first day of every month, all planned outages in the next 24 months; revisions as soon as reasonably practicable; a written reason when a change is submitted later than 3 months before the outage starts; delayed forced outages reported as soon as reasonably practicable and by recorded telephone line when less than 24 hours' notice; automatic forced outages reported by recorded telephone line and designated Derate-Forced or Outage-Forced; ISO outage cancellation directives only after posting an adequacy concern for at least 1 calendar week, contacting participants, CEO authorisation and no more than 90 days ahead; a cancelled participant submits a work description and incremental cost estimate and files a claim within 40 days. Revision history shows the 2020-09-16 version had the same requirements apart from one wording change in 2023.

sources.title: Information Document ID 2013-003R Outages (posted 2026-05-14)
sources.supports: Generation planned outages are submitted through the Energy Trading System and forced outages by telephone to a recorded AESO line; long lead time assets should submit a non-zero available capability from the first interval they can produce; AESO publishes Daily Outage, Monthly Outage (24 months) and 7 Day Hourly Available Capability reports from ETS submissions, updated every 5 to 10 minutes and at most 20 minutes; participants check a missing outage on the ETS Outage Scheduling tab. A later version than the 2019-2022 period; used only where it repeats rule text that was already in force.

sources.title: TransAlta Corporation 2021 Integrated Report (Form 6-K)
sources.publisher: TransAlta Corporation via U.S. SEC EDGAR
sources.supports: Adjusted availability 90.0 (2019), 90.7 (2020) and 86.6 percent (2021); Sundance 6, Keephills 2 and Keephills 3 converted to gas in Q1, Q2 and Q4 2021; planned conversion outages lowered 2021 availability; Alberta Gas production 8,691, 7,732 and 7,281 GWh in 2019-2021; power dispatched by AESO merit order; the company manages its offers internally and optimised production toward high-price periods in 2021. Only the first 100,000 characters of the filing were read.

assumptions: Hydro, wind and battery assets of 5 MW or more report outages under the same rule (wind since 2015), so planners also take requests from those sites; the thermal maintenance planner role stands in for all site planners.
The ETS entry is made by the outage planner using the pool participant's ETS account; in some companies the real-time desk enters it instead.
The mix of submission types (66 percent planned changes, 12 percent monthly refresh, 16 percent delayed forced, 6 percent AESO requests) is a tier C estimate.
The 2026 AESO information document is cited only where it repeats rule text in force in 2019-2022 (submission through the ETS, telephone notice) and for how the AESO reports are updated.
Loaded costs are taken from the organisation file (wage times 1.40).

The simulated median (about 4 days) is above the 3-day benchmark mainly because the monthly refresh path waits for month-end and the AESO-request path waits on the AESO; for ordinary planned changes the simulated time is close to the benchmark.
